newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia politician quits, anti-graft push grows.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia politician quits, anti-graft push grows.

text.p: The resignation of a senior Malaysian politician, who faces trial for trying to take almost $1 million out of Australia, was the latest step in a campaign against corruption in rapidly-growing Malaysia.
Muhammad Muhammad Taib, a vice president of Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's political party, quit as chief minister of central Selangor state on Saturday.
He was detained at Brisbane Internationl Airport on December 22 after the equivalent of US$940,000 in cash was found in his luggage and later charged with failing to declare an amount over A$5,000.
On Friday, a court in Brisbane charged him on a second count for making a false declaration. His trial was fixed to begin on August 19.

Mahathir announced the resignation after a leadership meeting of his United Malays National Organisation (UMNO). "We debated the matter and upon hearing the views of members, he (Muhammad) decided," Mahathir told reporters.
The case has dominated political talk in the capital since Muhammad's arrest.
Mahathir said it was hurting the party's image. "Members should not smear UMNO's name by doing something which casts negative aspersions on the party."
Muhammad was to announce on Monday whether he would step down as an UMNO vice president.
He had said he had taken the money to Australia to help his brother buy a house but was returning to Malaysia with it because the deal could not be concluded.

Muhammad was re-elected as one of three UMNO vice-presidents at last October's UMNO election convention, notable for an emotional speech by Mahathir on the evils of "money politics" -- vote buying, influence peddling, graft and other sins of corruption -- growing within the party.

Muhammad was part of Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim's so-called "vision team" when he was first elected vice-president in 1993. But political analysts say Muhammad has since tried to position himself as a loyal lieutenant of Mahathir as well.
"The feeling was that he should have done this (resign) much, much earlier," a senior Anwar aide told Reuters.
The resignation capped a week when corruption became a dominant theme in parliament.
A senior official in the Prime Minister's Department announced last week eight senior politicians in various states were being investigated by the Anti-Corruption Agency (ACA).
Anwar told parliament earlier in the week the government was unhappy with current measures to fight graft and said the ACA would receive more funds and manpower.
Money politics gained impetus in Malaysia in the late 1980s when the country embarked upon a decade-long course of eight percent annual growth that created millionaires overnight.
Privatised agencies were awarded to UMNO-linked businesses and a top position within the party was a ticket for access to lucrative contracts, licenses and shares.
A. Kadir Jasin, group editor of the pro-government New Straits Times, alluded to this in his Sunday column.
"In recent years, the Malaysia Incorporated policy, which brings together the government and the private sector, has proven to be a boon to the economy," Kadir said.
"But an increasing number of people are beginning to feel uncomfortable with what they see as too cosy a relationship among politicians, businessmen and top civil servants."
The issue has come to the fore during the past couple of years with several high-profile cases. In 1995, another chief minister and rising UMNO star was toppled in a corruption scandal.

Rahim Tamby Chik was forced to resign as chief minister of west coast Malacca state and UMNO youth wing chairman over allegations he had an affair with a schoolgirl and unrelated corruption charges -- all of which were later dropped.
In May of last year, Anwar told parliament that state-run Perwaja Steel had suffered accumulated losses of $1.16 billion, partly as a result of mismanagement and irregularities.
Perwaja's former managing director, Eric Chia, hand-picked by Mahathir to make Perwaja the centrepiece of Malaysia's industrialisation programme, resigned.
The Hong Kong-based Political and Economic Risk Consultancy, in a survey published two weeks ago, found Malaysia to be "in the middle of the pack when it comes to corruption in Asia".

It said recent cases showed "a steadily growing recognition that corrupt practices need to be rooted out if the country is to gain the international recognition for its economic acheivements it so obviously craves".
